“I examined the skull carefully. Its outer lines—the ones nearest the edges of the vellum—were much clearer than the rest. Evidently the heat had reached it unevenly or incompletely. I immediately lit a fire and exposed every part of the parchment to its glowing warmth. At first, this only darkened the faint outlines of the skull. But I kept at it, and eventually a figure appeared in the diagonally opposite corner. I initially took it for a goat; looking more closely, however, I became convinced that it was meant to represent a kid.”

“Ha, ha!” I said. “Of course, I have no business laughing at you—a million and a half is far too serious an amount to joke about. But you won’t be adding a third link to your chain of reasoning here. You can’t establish any special connection between pirates and a goat. Pirates have nothing to do with goats, you know; those belong to the farming world.”

“But I have just told you that the picture was not of a goat.”

“A kid, then. Practically the same thing.”

“Practically, but not exactly,” Legrand replied. “Perhaps you have heard of a certain Captain Kidd. I immediately understood the animal as a sort of signature made from a visual pun or picture-symbol. I say ‘signature’ because its position on the vellum suggested that interpretation. In much the same way, the skull in the diagonally opposite corner looked like a stamp or seal. What troubled me badly was the absence of everything else: the main content of this supposed document, the text that would fit the surrounding clues.”

“I suppose you expected a letter between the seal and the signature.”

“Something like that. The truth is, I had an overwhelming sense that some enormous good fortune lay ahead. I can hardly explain why. Perhaps it was more a wish than a conviction, after all. But Jupiter’s ridiculous claim that the beetle was solid gold had made a remarkable impression on my imagination. Then there was that whole sequence of accidents and coincidences, all of them so extraordinary. Do you see what sheer chance it was that everything happened on the only day of the entire year that has been, or is likely to be, cold enough for a fire? Without that fire, or without the dog coming in at precisely the moment it did, I would never have discovered the skull—and would therefore never have come into possession of the treasure.”

She was discovered dead in bed that morning, apparently without having suffered any pain. Sir Mathew Reid was summoned immediately, but naturally he could do nothing. Her burial was set for the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before her death, she had drawn up a will leaving Lord Arthur her small house in Curzon Street, along with her furniture, personal belongings, and paintings. The exceptions were her collection of miniatures, which she left to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, intended for Sybil Merton. The estate was not especially valuable, but Mr. Mansfield, her solicitor, was very keen for Lord Arthur to return immediately if he could. Numerous bills needed settling, and Lady Clementina had never kept proper accounts.

Lady Clementina’s generous remembrance moved Lord Arthur deeply, and he felt that Mr. Podgers had much to answer for. Yet his love for Sybil outweighed every other feeling, and the knowledge that he had fulfilled his duty brought him comfort and peace. By the time he reached Charing Cross, he was perfectly happy.

The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise never again to let anything separate them, and they set the wedding for June 7th. Life seemed bright and beautiful once more, and all his former happiness returned.

One day, however, while he was sorting through the Curzon Street house with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil, burning bundles of faded letters and clearing miscellaneous rubbish from drawers, Sybil suddenly gave a delighted little cry.

“What have you found, Sybil?” Lord Arthur asked, looking up from his work with a smile.

“This lovely little silver sweet box, Arthur. Isn’t it wonderfully quaint and Dutch? Please let me have it! I’m sure amethysts won’t suit me until I’m past eighty.”

It was the box that had contained the aconitine.

Lord Arthur flinched, and a slight blush coloured his face. He had almost completely forgotten his deed. It struck him as an odd coincidence that Sybil, for whose sake he had endured all that dreadful anxiety, should be the first to remind him of it.

“Of course you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.”

“Oh, thank you, Arthur! May I have the sweet as well? I never imagined Lady Clementina liked sweets. I thought she was much too intellectual.”

Lord Arthur’s face turned deathly pale as a terrible thought entered his mind.

But no—he could imagine something even more dazzling. He would become a pirate! That was the answer! Now he could see his future clearly, shining with a glory beyond anything he had dreamed. His name would travel around the world and make people tremble. How splendidly he would sail across the rolling seas in his swift, long, low ship with its black hull, the Spirit of the Storm, its terrible flag flying at the front! Then, at the height of his fame, he would suddenly return to the village and stride into church. He would be sun-browned and weather-beaten, dressed in a black velvet jacket and short breeches, tall heavy boots, and a scarlet sash. Large pistols would crowd his belt, a sword rusted from wicked deeds would hang at his side, and feathers would wave from his soft-brimmed hat. With his black skull-and-crossbones flag spread out, he would thrill to the whispers: “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, he had decided. This would be his life. He would run away from home to begin it, leaving the very next morning. So he must start preparing at once and gather his supplies. He walked to a nearby rotting log and dug beneath one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he struck a piece of wood that sounded hollow. Placing his hand on it, he solemnly spoke the magic words:

“Whatever hasn’t arrived here, come! Whatever is already here, stay!”

He scraped the earth away and uncovered a thin pine board. Lifting it, he revealed a neat little treasure chamber, its sides and floor also made of thin boards. Inside was a marble. Tom was utterly astonished. He scratched his head in confusion and said:

“Well, that beats everything!”

Then he flung the marble away irritably and stood thinking. A magical rule that he and all his friends had always trusted had failed. If you buried a marble, said the proper spells, and left it alone for two weeks, you were supposed to find every marble you had ever lost waiting there when you opened the hiding place with the words he had just used. It did not matter how far apart those marbles had been. Yet this time the magic had plainly failed. All Tom’s beliefs were shaken. He had often heard stories of the charm working, but never of its failing. He forgot that he himself had tried it several times and afterward could never find the hiding places. He puzzled over it for a while, then decided some witch must have interfered and spoiled the spell.
